title: Does paying a permit consultant get a permit faster?
question: Do permits handled by a paid permit consultant get through faster than like permits without one?
finding: 12,196 building permits filed 2015 to 2024 list a permit consultant or expediter (4.3% of all; 30% of full-review jobs of $5 million and over, 9.7% of those under $50,000). Set against like permits of the same kind, cost band and year, the answer is mixed: on jobs sent for full plan review the consultant's permit came out ahead (229 days against 289), but across all permits it was faster only 44% of the time (alterations approved at the counter: median 14 days against 15 for like permits without one; alterations sent for full plan review: median 229 days against 289 for like permits without one; new buildings: median 303 days against 306 for like permits without one). In their own filings, 46 consultants and firms reported $6.7 million in client fees.
how: Each permit with a consultant was ranked among issued permits without one of the same permit type, cost band, filing year and plans-or-no-plans; 0.5 means no difference, lower means faster. The table lists consultants and firms with 25 or more ranked full-review or new-building permits, where waits are long enough to matter. Fees are what consultants reported on the Ethics Commission's quarterly Form 3410B ('amount of compensation'), read from the text of the filed forms.
limits: Hiring a permit consultant is common, and consultants must register and report. Professionals file cleaner plans, know which review path to ask for, and may pick jobs that are easy to move, so a gap is a question about fairness of access and not proof of favours. Consultant names are typed in by hand and vary; unnamed helpers are not captured. Fees could be read from only some filings (scanned paper forms are not readable), cover all permit work and not only building permits, and several filers write that they report only projects over $1 million.
